summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office reviewed AI implementation across 23 major federal agencies and found that 20 of those agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Per GAO, the reported applications ranged from analyzing drone photographs and large datasets to identifying border activities through cameras and radar and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number of use cases. Critically, most of those use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in active production, and in only about 200 instances were agencies reported to be currently using AI operationally.

GAO's review identified meaningful gaps in how agencies are managing and documenting their AI activity. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the remaining 15 had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data, including missing lifecycle stage information and cases where reported AI uses were later determined by the agencies themselves not to qualify as AI. Per GAO, ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing consistent management of AI risks and benefits across the federal government.

On the funding side, GAO noted that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling substantial federal commitment even as implementation lagged behind policy ambition. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, representing two of the more complete compliance efforts GAO identified. The Office of Science and Technology Policy, however, did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements, adding further coordination risk.

The regulatory and legislative environment surrounding government AI use is active and growing. The site's own AI Laws section tracks 3,013 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, giving a real-time picture of the legislative pressure that agencies at every level are navigating. OECD.AI, the Policy Observatory operated by the OECD, monitors national AI strategies and public-sector initiatives across member and partner countries, tracking ethical frameworks alongside deployment activity, while Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption for cross-national comparison. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries a government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement trends, and notes in its current edition a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governing frameworks are to manage it.

For any organization or agency weighing deployment in a government context, the GAO findings are the most concrete available benchmark: actual federal adoption is narrower than the headline inventory count suggests, compliance requirements are real and not uniformly met, and the absence of government-wide acquisition guidance means each agency is largely navigating procurement on its own. The density of active legislation tracked across 53 jurisdictions also signals that the regulatory baseline is still being written, making governance documentation and accurate use-case inventories practical necessities rather than optional overhead.
